For over fifty one Sundays, here in the Church of Holy Cross we have heard the good news of Christ among us declaring over and over again in many ways and by many deeds his unconditional love for us. We have heard howfar he will go to both embrace and chase us, even when we flee from him. Today on this final Sunday of the Church’s year the equation is reversed. We are asked how we have embraced and chased Jesus in the poor and the needy. It is a sober thought that on the last day we shall be judged. Someone outside of us will judge us. This very notion grates on our modern sensitivities. In our value-neutral society where we like to believe that there is no higher standard of judgement than our own self- measurements, this gospel today as the effrontery to remind us that we shall be judged by Another. We declare this reality of judgement when we pray in the Creed: “He will come to judge the living and the dead” In this Gospel today (Matthew 25:31-46) we are told that we shall be judged in according to our reaction to human need. God’s judgement does not depend on the knowledge we have gained, or the fame that we have gathered, or on the fortune that we have collected, but on the help we have given. Jesus tells us it must be help in the simple things - giving a hungry person a meal, a thirsty person a drink, welcoming the stranger, cheering the sick and visiting the prisoner. These are things that anyone of us can do. We hear in the Gospel those who helped did not think that they were helping Christ.they helped because they could not stop themselves from helping. It is the natural, instinctive, quite uncalculating reaction of a loving heart. Jesus confronts us with this truth, that all such help which is given to Himself, and all such help which is withheld from Him. If we really wish to delight a parent’s heart, if we really wish to move them to gratitude, then the best way to do it is help his/her child. God is the great Father, and way to delight the heart of God is to help his children, who are our fellow men and women. It is a grace that before Mass, we sometimes pray .” 1 have sinned through my own fault, in my thoughts and in my words, in what I have done and in what | HAVE FAILED TO DO” Those good things that we failed to do are called the sins of omission. In the New Testament, the classic example given by Jesus is the account of the Good Samaritan. After a man had been beaten and left in need of help, the first two men to pass by—a priest and a Levite, both of whom knew better—failed to act. The third man, a Samaritan, stopped to show compassion to the man in need (Luke 10:30-37). There was no sin committed in today’s Gospel against these needy people—they were not intentionally starved or deprived of their clothing. But the sin of omission was committed when those who could have provided for them chose not to. Our Lord is the Servant King, the Good Shepherd and shows us the way to act and from Ezekiel in today’s first reading we hear the Lord say: will look after the lost one, bring back the stray, bandage the wounded and make the weak strong. I shall watch over the fat and healthy. I shall be a true shepherd to them” ( Ezekiel 34:16)
